cards.b: Eight planets orbit in nearly the same plane, in the same direction as the Sun spins. That is not an accident. It is a fingerprint of how the Solar System was born, and the same process now appears to be going on around other young stars.

About 4.6 billion years ago, a cloud of gas and dust, mostly hydrogen and helium plus the ashes of earlier stars, began to collapse under its own gravity, perhaps triggered by a nearby supernova. This is the nebular hypothesis, proposed by Immanuel Kant (1755) and Pierre-Simon Laplace (1796).

As the cloud shrank it spun faster, like a skater pulling in her arms (conservation of angular momentum), and flattened into a disc. Most of the mass fell to the centre and became the Sun. The leftover disc, the protoplanetary disc, carried a small fraction of mass, about 1 percent, and almost all the angular momentum.

This explains the flat orbits and shared direction.

Dust grains stuck together, growing into pebbles, then kilometre-size planetesimals, then protoplanets, a process called accretion. In the hot inner disc only rock and metal survived, so rocky planets stayed small. Beyond the frost line (around 3 to 5 AU), ice added mass: giant cores grew and captured gas. Gas giants had only a few million years before the young Sun blew the gas away.

The system was violent. Jupiter may have migrated inward and then back out, a model called the Grand Tack, scattering material. Planets collided: Earth was struck by Theia, making the Moon; Uranus may have been knocked over. About 4 billion years ago, a bombardment of leftover bodies cratered the inner planets. Water may have arrived partly from asteroids and comets.
Rocky planets inside, giants outside, a belt of unformed material between Mars and Jupiter, and icy leftovers beyond Neptune. Earth was born about 4.54 billion years ago.

cards.h: Meteorites, Moon rocks and other discs
cards.b: Clair Patterson dated meteorites in 1956 using uranium-lead decay: 4.55 billion years. The oldest solid grains (calcium-aluminium inclusions) are 4.567 billion years. Radio telescopes like ALMA now photograph discs around young stars; the 2014 image of HL Tauri shows gaps where baby planets sweep a path. Simple rules predicted exoplanets, but we found surprises, like hot Jupiters, which forced the migration idea.

• 'Planets formed from a piece torn from the Sun.' That tidal theory fails: they formed from the shared disc.
  • 'Earth was always like this.' It started as molten rock.
  • 'Our system is typical.' Many exoplanet systems look very different.

The Physical Research Laboratory (PRL) in Ahmedabad, founded in 1947 by Vikram Sarabhai with K.R. Ramanathan, studies meteorites, isotopes and planetary science, including the PARAS spectrograph that found an exoplanet in 2018. Jayant Narlikar founded IUCAA, Pune, in 1988 to advance research on how cosmic structures form. Chandrayaan lunar data help test impact history, since the Moon preserves the early bombardment.

• The Solar System formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud.
  • Spin flattened it into a disc, explaining flat, same-direction orbits.
  • The frost line separates rocky and giant planets.
  • Meteorite dating and ALMA images support the model; migration adds the messy details.

Think about it: (1) Why do all planets orbit the same way? (2) What would you expect to find around a very young star?
